pageTitle: Good to Know: Traveling Japan as Americans

items.title: Expect real winter, but dry
items.body: February is one of the coldest months in most of the trip's destinations, but also one of the driest and clearest — Tokyo, Kyoto, and Osaka average highs around 50°F (10°C) and lows near freezing, with Kyushu (Fukuoka, Beppu) running a few degrees milder. Snow is possible but usually light and doesn't stick for long in these cities, except in Hokkaido, where the friend's snowboarding leg will see proper snow cover.

items.title: Layer, don't just bring one heavy coat
items.body: Indoor spaces in Japan — trains, restaurants, shops, hotel lobbies — are often heated quite warm, so a single bulky coat gets uncomfortable indoors. A base layer, a mid layer (fleece or light sweater), and a proper warm outer coat that's easy to take off and carry is more practical than one heavyweight parka worn all day.

items.title: Comfortable walking shoes are non-negotiable
items.body: This trip involves a lot of walking — temple grounds, train station transfers (some Tokyo stations require 10+ minutes of walking between platforms), and full days of city exploring. Broken-in, comfortable shoes matter more than fashion here. Worth noting for temple/shrine visits and any traditional restaurant with tatami seating: shoes come off, so shoes that slip on/off easily (rather than complicated laces) save a lot of minor hassle repeated throughout the day.

items.title: Bring a scarf, gloves, and a hat
items.body: Wind chill matters more than the raw temperature for a lot of outdoor activities on this trip — Fushimi Inari's mountain trail, Mount Tsurumi's summit, ferry crossings on open water. Small, packable accessories make a bigger comfort difference than they might suggest.

items.title: What NOT to overpack
items.body: Heavy snow boots aren't necessary outside the Hokkaido leg — regular winter shoes handle the rest of the trip fine. Umbrellas are easy and cheap to buy on the ground in Japan (convenience stores sell simple ones for a few hundred yen) if rain or snow catches anyone off guard, so there's no need to pack a bulky one preemptively.

items.title: Modesty note for temples and shrines
items.body: There's no strict dress code enforced at most temples and shrines, but overly revealing clothing can draw stares or feel out of place given the reflective, quiet atmosphere of these sites — not a hard rule, just worth keeping in mind when packing for the Kyoto/Nara-heavy days specifically.

packingChecklist.title: Packing list
packingChecklist.intro: Use a mix-and-match winter capsule: pack for about 7 days, do laundry once during the two-week trip, and use the same core kit for Maddi's one-week visit without needing a laundry stop.

items.label: 1 warm, weather-resistant winter coat with room for layers
2 sweaters or fleece mid-layers for insulating over base layers
4–5 versatile long-sleeve tops in a mix-and-match color palette
3 bottoms: 2 comfortable walking pants plus 1 flexible backup
7 pairs of underwear and 7 pairs of warm walking socks
1 set of sleepwear or comfortable lounge clothes
1 pair of broken-in walking shoes that are easy to slip off
1 optional lightweight backup pair, if luggage space allows
1 scarf, 1 pair of gloves, and 1 warm hat
1 compact umbrella or room to buy one in Japan
Small day bag with room for water, layers, and purchases
Passport, copies, travel confirmations, and emergency contacts
Personal medications and a small travel first-aid kit
Phone chargers, battery pack, and necessary adapters
Laundry bag and a few detergent sheets for one mid-trip wash
Private-bath plan instead of a swimsuit for traditional onsen

items.title: Japan is far more cash-based than expected
items.body: Despite its high-tech reputation, Japan still runs heavily on cash — many smaller restaurants, temples, older shops, and some ryokan (especially outside major cities like the Beppu/Yufuin/Matsuyama legs of this trip) don't accept cards at all. Carrying cash isn't a backup plan here, it's often the primary plan.

items.title: 7-Eleven ATMs are the reliable way to get cash
items.body: 7-Eleven convenience store ATMs reliably accept foreign cards (Visa, Mastercard, major US bank cards) and are everywhere, including in smaller towns — more reliable for foreign card withdrawals than many actual bank ATMs, which can be surprisingly hit-or-miss with international cards.

items.title: IC cards (Suica/Pasmo) for transit and small purchases
items.body: A rechargeable IC card (Suica or Pasmo, functionally interchangeable) works as a tap-to-pay card for nearly all trains, subways, and buses nationwide, and doubles as payment at convenience stores, some vending machines, and many casual restaurants. iPhone users can add Suica directly to Apple Wallet before the trip and top it up digitally; a physical card is the simpler option for Android users or anyone who'd rather not deal with the digital setup. Either way, this removes the need to buy individual paper train tickets for every single ride.

items.title: Tipping is not customary — and can be awkward
items.body: Tipping isn't part of Japanese service culture and can actually cause confusion or mild discomfort if attempted at restaurants, taxis, or hotels — excellent service is the cultural default, not something signaled with an extra payment. Exceptional service is better acknowledged with a sincere thank-you than a tip.

items.title: Tax-free shopping for tourists
items.body: Many stores offer tax-free (consumption tax exempt) shopping for foreign tourists on purchases over a minimum amount (typically ¥5,000), usually processed at a dedicated tax-free counter with passport in hand. Worth keeping the passport accessible while shopping, not just for entry/exit.

items.title: eSIM or pocket WiFi before arrival
items.body: US phone plans typically don't include Japan coverage by default. The two common solutions: an eSIM (installed digitally before departure, no physical SIM swap needed on compatible phones) or a pocket WiFi device (rented at the airport or beforehand, shared across the whole group's devices on one connection) — pocket WiFi is often the better call for a group traveling together, since one device covers everyone rather than each person needing their own eSIM.

items.title: Free WiFi is inconsistent
items.body: Unlike some countries, free public WiFi in Japan is patchy outside of major train stations, some convenience stores, and hotels — don't count on it as a primary connectivity plan for navigation or translation on the go.

items.title: Trains run on time, to the minute
items.body: Japanese trains are famous for extreme punctuality — arriving even a couple minutes late to a platform can mean missing a specific train, especially for reserved shinkansen seats. Building in buffer time before train connections, especially with luggage, is worth it.

items.title: JR Pass — price this out for the route
items.body: The Japan Rail Pass offers unlimited travel on JR trains (including most shinkansen) for a fixed multi-day period, and given this trip's heavy use of the Tokaido-Sanyo Shinkansen corridor (Kyoto, Osaka, Nagoya, Hiroshima, Fukuoka all connect via this line), it's worth calculating whether the pass cost beats buying individual tickets for this specific set of long-distance legs. Note it doesn't cover the ferry legs (Hiroshima-Matsuyama, Matsuyama-Beppu) or most local subway lines.

items.title: Priority seating and phone etiquette on trains
items.body: Talking on the phone is considered rude on trains and buses — texting silently is fine, but voice calls are generally avoided. Priority seats near train doors are reserved for elderly, pregnant, disabled, or injured passengers even if empty, and it's considered impolite to sit there otherwise.

items.title: No eating on local trains (shinkansen is different)
items.body: Eating on local commuter trains and subways is generally considered bad etiquette. The shinkansen (bullet train) is the exception — eating a bento box while traveling is completely normal and even a bit of a tradition, especially on longer legs like Kyoto to Hiroshima.

items.title: Shoes off indoors — know when it applies
items.body: Shoes come off when entering someone's home, most ryokan, temples with interior access, traditional restaurants with tatami seating, and some smaller shops — look for a genkan (a slightly recessed entryway with a shoe rack or shelf) as the visual cue. Slip-on shoes save real hassle given how often this comes up throughout a single day.

items.title: Bowing is common but not obligatory for tourists
items.body: A slight nod of the head in place of a full bow is completely acceptable for foreign visitors and won't come across as rude — Japanese people generally don't expect tourists to master bowing etiquette, and over-performing it can feel more awkward than a simple nod.

items.title: Public trash bins are rare — carry your trash
items.body: Public trash cans are surprisingly uncommon on Japanese streets, so the norm is carrying trash — food wrappers, empty bottles — until reaching a convenience store, train station, or home base with a bin. Worth keeping a small bag on hand for this rather than being caught without an option.

items.title: Quiet, orderly public behavior is the norm
items.body: Loud conversation, phone calls in public transit, and eating while walking down the street are all mildly frowned upon in a way that's more strictly observed than in the US — not illegal or aggressively policed, just noticeably different from American norms, and worth being aware of rather than standing out unintentionally.

items.title: Queueing is taken seriously
items.body: Lines for trains, elevators, popular food stalls, and store openings are orderly and respected — cutting or crowding a line is a more noticeable faux pas here than in many other countries. Train platforms often have marked lines showing exactly where to queue for each car door.

items.title: Vending machines and convenience stores (konbini) are genuinely excellent
items.body: Vending machines (hot and cold drinks, sometimes hot food) are everywhere, and convenience stores (7-Eleven, Lawson, FamilyMart) sell surprisingly good, fresh food — onigiri, sandwiches, hot items — not the lower-quality gas-station-snack reputation convenience stores have in the US. Worth using them as a legitimate meal option, not just an emergency backup.

items.title: Onsen etiquette (relevant for the Beppu/Yufuin leg)
items.body: Wash and rinse thoroughly at the shower stations before entering the communal bath water — the bath itself is for soaking, not washing. Swimsuits are not worn in traditional onsen (nudity is standard and not sexualized in this context), and small modesty towels are meant to be kept out of the actual bathwater, typically placed on the head or the side. Given the earlier research on tattoo policies, this is also the context where private family baths (kashikiri-buro) become the practical workaround if needed.

items.title: US passport holders: visa-free entry
items.body: US citizens can enter Japan visa-free for short-term tourism (up to 90 days) — no visa application needed for this trip's length. Passport should have at least 6 months of validity remaining beyond the travel dates as a general best practice, even though Japan technically only requires validity through the length of stay.

items.title: Visit Japan Web — optional but worth doing
items.body: Visit Japan Web is an official portal that lets travelers pre-register immigration and customs information online, generating QR codes that speed up the airport arrival process (a 'Fast Track' option at major airports). It's not mandatory — paper forms and standard processing are still available — but pre-registering (ideally a few days before departure) meaningfully cuts down arrival-line time, worth doing given how many separate international/domestic connections this trip involves. A digital travel-authorization requirement (similar to the US's ESTA) is planned but not launching until 2028, so it doesn't affect this trip.

items.title: A small departure/tourist tax applies
items.body: Japan charges a small international tourist tax (around ¥1,000 at the time of this trip; a larger increase to ¥3,000 doesn't take effect until July 2026, after this trip) added automatically to outbound flight costs — not something requiring separate payment or action, just worth knowing it's baked into the ticket price rather than a surprise fee at the airport.

items.title: Emergency numbers
items.body: Police: 110. Fire and ambulance: 119. Both can be reached from any phone, though English-language support may be limited on these lines — Japan Visitor Hotline (050-3816-2787) offers 24/7 multilingual tourist assistance for both emergencies and general travel questions, and is a genuinely useful number to have saved before landing.

items.title: Power outlets and voltage
items.body: Japan uses 100V (lower than the US's 120V) with the same two-flat-prong plug shape as US outlets (Type A), so most US electronics work without an adapter, though very sensitive or high-wattage devices may run slightly differently on the lower voltage. A universal adapter isn't strictly necessary for most standard phone chargers and laptop chargers, but worth double-checking anything unusual before packing.

items.title: Record tourism numbers mean book ahead
items.body: Japan saw a record number of international visitors in 2025, meaning popular restaurants, ryokan, and reservation-based attractions (like Ghibli Park, already flagged elsewhere as time-sensitive) are filling up faster than in past years. Building in advance reservations wherever possible, rather than assuming walk-in availability, is more important now than it might have been on an earlier trip to Japan.

items.title: English signage is common in major cities, less so in small towns
items.body: Tokyo, Kyoto, and Osaka have extensive English signage in train stations and major attractions, but this thins out noticeably in smaller stops on this trip's route — Matsuyama, Beppu/Yufuin, and parts of Nara and Fukuoka. A translation app (Google Translate's camera feature for menus/signs works well offline with downloaded language packs) is worth having ready rather than assuming English will be available everywhere.

items.title: A few basic phrases go a long way
items.body: Arigatou gozaimasu (thank you), sumimasen (excuse me / sorry, also used to get someone's attention), and eigo wa daijoubu desu ka (is English okay?) cover a surprising amount of ground. Attempting even basic Japanese is generally well-received rather than expected — it's the effort that matters, not fluency.
